title: Runbook Actions — Admin utility catalog, CLI wrappers, and event-driven automation
creator: Maya Chen
description: Synthesize existing ad-hoc admin utilities and runbooks into a discoverable 'Runbook Actions' catalog: canonicalize small operational tasks as idempotent CLI wrappers and event-driven tasks, make them runnable from the admin console and Slack, and wire them into the runbooks-as-tasks framework. Goal is to reduce mean time-to-resolution for common incidents by surfacing vetted actions that perform safety-checked operations (e.g., resync cache shards, rotate a dedicated pool, bump KV cache TTLs, revoke user tokens). Deliverables: (1) catalog schema and metadata tags, (2) 10 high-priority action implementations with tests and dry-run modes, (3) admin-console UI hook + Slack slash command, (4) runtime permissions model and audit log integration.
acceptance_criteria: Action catalog schema published in Confluence with metadata fields: id, description, safety_level, dry_run_supported, owner, required_permissions, estimated_runtime
10 actions implemented and merged with unit+integration tests and CI gating (see PRs)
All actions support a --dry-run flag and return structured JSON for console rendering
Admin console lists actions with owner/bounds and a run button that opens a confirmation flow
Slack slash command /ops-run <action-id> triggers the dry-run by default and requires interactive confirmation for destructive actions
Audit logs show action start/end, parameters, and invoking principal in KMS-backed audit stream
risks: Actions that mutate state could be used incorrectly — mitigated by dry-run and interactive confirmations
Permissions model complexity across Hosted/Dedicated/Private may require per-deployment RBAC rules
Telemetry gap: some low-level primitives lack tracing so we may not capture full end-to-end latency
Rolling back partial failures for multi-step actions will need compensating actions which add complexity
implementation_notes: Use existing opsctl binary as the runtime for actions where possible; add an 'action' subcommand and a standardized JSON output format
Keep action handlers small, single-responsibility, and idempotent; prefer typed parameter schemas validated at invocation time
Integrate with the new runbooks-as-tasks message format (see runbook DSL v2) so actions can be composed into playlists
Authorization: reuse platform service-account model + map console users to short-lived tokens issued by the admin control plane
Observability: emit action.start/action.end spans and correlate with request_id for easier debugging
comments: 2026-01-18 — Kickoff: scoped to 10 actions for initial rollout. Agreed on dry-run default and interactive confirmation for destructive ops. Action list curated from incident postmortems (cache hotkeys, pool recycle, model pin).

2026-01-22 — Design review: PM suggested grouping actions by safety_level and exposing 'learning mode' so new actions run in dry-run for 24h in prod. UX asked for single-click rollback when available.

2026-01-30 — Engineering sync: implemented initial action-schema and proto for JSON output. Prototype CLI wrapper created in branch feature/runbook-actions. PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/1092

2026-02-02 — Security review kickoff: SecOps requested mandatory audit metadata and an allowlist for high-privilege actions in Dedicated/Private deployments. Planning extra gating for admin-2026.02 release.

2026-02-05 — QA update: 4 actions have unit + integration tests (cache-resync, pool-drain, token-revoke, quota-reset). Dry-run verified against staging dashboard: https://dash.redwood.internal/d/ops/actions-runbook-playground
Follow-ups: (1) Add e2e test harness that runs dry-run then real-run in sandbox, (2) Finalize RBAC mapping for private customers, (3) Draft runbook->action migration guide for on-call teams
